blocks.text: Once you can trace the example without looking at the code, write the implementation yourself. Compare it with a simple loop on new inputs. The links offer another explanation; this lesson’s prose, examples and code were written for Erdene Club.

Sorting costs $O(n\log n)$. The following scan visits each event once and performs constant work, costing $O(n)$. Together they are $O(n\log n)$; do not omit sorting and claim linear time. Only already finish-sorted input permits a linear scan alone.

This implementation takes the vector by value, so it uses an additional $O(n)$ copy besides the caller's input, plus sorting stack space. Sorting in place avoids the copy, with typical introsort using about $O(\log n)$ stack. A short function can still allocate a large copy.

The proof no longer applies when events carry weights and total weight is the objective. Events $[0,3),[3,6)$ of weight $2$ each beat a weight-$100$ event $[0,6)$ by count but not by weight. The exchange does not preserve the objective, so another method such as DP is needed.

sections.title: 13. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: For a new greedy problem ask: what breaks if I replace a choice in an optimal solution with mine? Separately check that future feasibility does not shrink and that the objective does not worsen. A small oracle enumerating subsets of two to six elements helps find counterexamples to a proposed rule.
Use it for maximum unweighted interval count. With different values, earliest finishing does not ensure maximum total value; weighted interval DP is needed. Correctness depends on the objective.

Хариуг шууд байгуулж олох хэцүү бол “хариу $L$-ээс ихгүй байж болох уу?” гэж асуу. Энд checker нь хэсэг бүрийн sum $L$-ээс ихгүй байхаар хамгийн ихдээ $k$ хэсэг гаргаж болох эсэхийг хэлнэ.

en.title: Binary search on the answer
en.summary: Test whether a proposed answer is sufficient instead of computing the optimum directly.

blocks.text: Split $a=[2,4,3,5]$ into at most $2$ contiguous parts, minimizing the largest part sum. Splitting into $[2,4]$ and $[3,5]$ gives sums $6,8$, so $8$ is feasible.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Enumerating splits can be expensive. For a fixed limit, scan left to right and greedily fill each part until the next element would exceed it.
Search between the largest element and the total sum for the first feasible limit. Nonnegative elements are required for this greedy checker.
When constructing the optimum directly is hard, ask whether an answer at most $L$ is possible. The checker asks whether the array can be divided into at most $k$ segments, each with sum at most $L$.

The checker fills each segment as far as possible, starting a new one only when the next value would exceed the limit. With nonnegative values, cutting earlier cannot reduce the remaining work, so the longest feasible prefix minimizes segment count.

If $L$ is feasible, any larger limit is feasible using the same partition. The optimum is the false-to-true boundary. Start between the maximum element and total sum: no segment can fit an oversized element, while the total always fits one segment.

items: $\mathrm{can}(L)$ tests whether at most $k$ parts can each have sum at most $L$.
Monotonicity: if a limit works, every larger limit also works.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Do not test every possible limit separately. Monotonic feasibility lets one check discard half the remaining limits. However, each check scans the array, so its cost must be included.

The checker processes every element once: $O(n)$. Searching the integer interval from the maximum element to total sum $S$ needs $O(\log(S+1))$ checks. Total time is $O(n\log(S+1))$, not merely $O(\log S)$.
Example: an answer interval from $0$ to $1023$ needs about $10$ feasibility checks instead of $1024$. If each check scans $1000$ elements, the scale is $10^4$ visits instead of $10^6$.
Prove both the checker and monotonicity first. This lesson’s greedy checker assumes nonnegative array values.

Frequency array-г хамгийн их утгын хэмжээгээр гаргах боломжгүй байж болно. Зөвхөн input-д байгаа утгуудад index өгснөөр array-ийн урт хамгийн ихдээ $n$ болно.
Array-ийн copy-г sort хийнэ, давхардлыг арилгана. Анхны элемент бүрийн тэр жагсаалт дахь байрлалыг lower_bound-оор олно. Ижил утга ижил rank-тай.

Coordinate compression нь absolute value-ийн оронд утгын sorted rank ашиглах арга. Харьцуулалтын дараалал хадгалагдана: $x<y$ бол rank($x$)<rank($y$), $x=y$ бол rank ижил. Энэ нь хэмжээ ихтэй coordinate-д жижиг array index өгөх боломж олгоно.

Алхамууд: input copy-г sort, duplicate-ийг unique хийж хас, утга бүрийг lower_bound-аар ол. Rank-ийн хамгийн их утга distinct count-оос нэгээр бага. Original array-ийн order-ийг өөрчлөхгүйгээр rank array-г тусад нь гаргана.

Compression тоон зайг хадгалахгүй. $7$ ба $100$ rank $0,1$ боллоо гээд хоорондын distance $1$ болсон гэж бодож болохгүй. Distance, урт, interval-ийн хоосон зай хэрэгтэй бол sorted original values-ийг буцааж ашиглана.

en.summary: Replace large values by small indices while preserving their order.

blocks.text: In $a=[100,5,100,-2]$, only three values are distinct. Sort them as $[-2,5,100]$ and assign indices $0,1,2$, obtaining $[2,1,2,0]$.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Allocating an array up to the largest value may be impossible. Assign indices only to values present in the input, keeping the array length at most $n$.
Sort a copy, remove duplicates, and find each original value’s index with lower_bound. Equal values receive equal ranks.

Coordinate compression replaces a value with its sorted rank. It preserves order and equality: $x<y$ implies rank($x$)<rank($y$), and equal values share a rank. Huge coordinates can then index small arrays.

Sort a copy, remove duplicates with unique, and locate each original value using lower_bound. The largest rank is one below the distinct count. Build a separate rank array without changing original order.
Compression does not preserve numeric distances. If $7$ and $100$ become ranks $0,1$, their original distance is not $1$. Keep the sorted original values when lengths or gaps matter.

items: A rank is the position among sorted distinct values.
This compression is not hashing; it uses sorting and binary search.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: The coordinate-compression code does not scan the sorted list from the beginning for every value. It prepares sorted distinct values, then uses lower_bound to find each rank by binary search.

Copying costs $O(n)$, sorting $O(n\log n)$ and deduplication $O(n)$. Then $n$ binary searches each cost $O(\log n)$, giving $O(n\log n)$ overall. Even huge numeric values produce at most $n$ distinct ranks.
Example: $[10^9,7,10^9,100]$ has the distinct sorted list $[7,100,10^9]$. It needs three ranks, not an array of $10^9$ positions.
Compression saves storage that would depend on the numeric range. It still sorts, so it is not a linear-time method; this reference does not use a hash table.

en.title: Tree basics — parent, depth and subtree
en.summary: Choose a root, orient the tree conceptually, and compute subtree sizes with DFS.

blocks.text: Edges are $(0,1),(0,2),(1,3),(1,4)$. With root $0$, vertex $1$ has subtree $\{1,3,4\}$ of size $3$. The root depth is $0$, while vertex $3$ has depth $2$.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Instead of recounting descendants separately for every vertex, combine children’s subtree sizes. Their subtrees do not overlap.
Pass the incoming parent to DFS and skip that neighbor. After each child call finishes, add its subtree size to the current vertex’s size.

A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph with $n-1$ edges. Choosing a root turns the neighbour towards the root into the parent and the others into children. Changing the root may change parents, depths and subtrees without changing edges.
Depth is the edge distance from the root. A subtree includes its vertex and all descendants. Its size is $sz[v]=1+\sum sz[u]$ over children: count itself and disjoint child subtrees.

Skipping the parent suffices in a tree because there are no other visited neighbours. Add a child’s size after its recursive call returns; before that it is unfinished. This postorder pattern is the basis of tree DP.

items: A tree is a connected acyclic undirected graph and has $n-1$ edges.
Parent is the neighbor toward the root; depth counts edges from the root.
A subtree contains its root vertex and all descendants.

Leaf $2$ has size $1$ and depth $1$.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Running a fresh DFS for every subtree repeatedly counts the same descendants for different ancestors. One postorder DFS computes children first and reuses their sizes at the parent.
Each vertex is called once and computes its size once. A tree’s $n-1$ edges make $2(n-1)$ adjacency entries, so all neighbour scans cost $O(n)$. Adding a completed child size is constant work.
Example: separately counting each subtree of a $5$-vertex chain needs $5+4+3+2+1=15$ visits. One DFS computes exactly $5$ vertex answers once each.
Skipping the parent is sufficient for a tree, but not for a cyclic graph without visited tracking. A long tree can still need $O(n)$ recursion stack.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Useful for subtree DP, rooted-tree queries and LCA preparation. Having $n-1$ edges alone does not prove a tree; connectivity also matters. Parent skipping alone does not protect a cyclic graph from repeated recursion.

blocks.text: $n$ гишгүүртэй шатаар нэг удаад $1$ эсвэл $2$ гишгүүр ахиж гарна. Ялгаатай хэдэн дарааллаар оройд хүрэх вэ? $n=4$ үед $1+1+1+1$, $1+1+2$, $1+2+1$, $2+1+1$, $2+2$ гэсэн таван арга байна. Энд $1+2$ ба $2+1$ нь өөр дараалал гэдгийг эхлээд тогтооё.

Бүх алхмын дарааллыг recursion-аар үүсгэвэл зөв. Гэхдээ $5$ гишгүүр үлдсэн ижил асуудлыг өөр өөр замаар ирэх бүрд дахин бодно. DP хэрэгтэй болсон шалтгаан нь recursion өөрөө бус, ижил үлдсэн асуудал олон дахин гарч байгаад оршино.
$n$ шатанд нэг эсвэл хоёр алхмаар өгсөнө. $n=3$ үед $1+1+1$, $1+2$, $2+1$ гэсэн $3$ арга байна. $n$ том бол хэдэн арга вэ?

State-аа бүтэн өгүүлбэрээр тодорхойл: $dp_i$ нь яг $i$ гишгүүрийг туулах алхмын дарааллын тоо. Ирээдүйн боломжийг шийдэхэд өмнөх алхмуудын бүх түүх биш, үлдсэн зай л хэрэгтэй. Энэ нь ижил state-уудыг нэгтгэж болох шалтгаан.

Сүүлийн алхмаар нь ангилъя. Сүүлийн алхам $1$ байсан бүх дараалал нь $i-1$ гишгүүрт хүрсэн нэг дарааллын ард $1$ залгасантай адил. Сүүлийн алхам $2$ байсан нь $i-2$-ын араас $2$ залгасан. Иймээс $dp_i=dp_{i-1}+dp_{i-2}$; зөвхөн $i\ge2$ үед хоёр дахь гишүүн орно.

$dp_0=1$: огт алхахгүй хоосон дараалал нэг бий. Үүнийг $0$ гэвэл $dp_1$, $dp_2$ цаашлаад бүх тоо буруу болно. $i$-г өсөхөөр боловсруулахад хамаарах жижиг state-ууд аль хэдийн бэлэн. Энэ dependency order нь bottom-up DP-ийн үндэс.
Сүүлийн алхмыг $1$ эсвэл $2$ гэж салгасан recursion бичиж болно. Гэхдээ жижиг $n$-ийн хариуг дахин дахин асууна. Нэгэнт бодсон жижиг хариуг array-д хадгалъя.
Сүүлийн алхам $1$ бол өмнө нь $i-1$, $2$ бол $i-2$ дээр байсан. Энэ хоёр бүлэг давхцахгүй тул тоонуудыг нэмнэ. $\mathrm{dp}[i]=\mathrm{dp}[i-1]+\mathrm{dp}[i-2]$.

DP-г formula цээжлэхээс биш state-ийн утга бичихээс эхэл. Энд $dp[i]$ нь яг $i$ гишгүүр хүрэх ordered алхмын дарааллын тоо. $1,2$ ба $2,1$ өөр зам. Зөвхөн сүүлийн хэдэн алхмыг мэдэхэд цаашдын боломж бүрэн тодорхой болох state сонгоно.

Сүүлийн алхам $1$ эсвэл $2$. Эхний бүлэг өмнөх $i-1$-д хүрсэн зам бүрт $1$ нэмснээс, хоёр дахь нь $i-2$-д хүрсэн зам бүрт $2$ нэмснээс үүснэ. Бүлгүүд сүүлийн алхмаараа ялгаатай тул давхцахгүй: $dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]$.

Base case $dp[0]$=$1$ нь “юу ч хийхгүй” ганц зам. Энэ base байснаар эхний алхмууд ч ижил recurrence-ээр гарна. Өсөх $i$ дарааллаар бодвол унших өмнөх state-үүд бэлэн байна. Memoization ижил state-ийг хэрэгтэй үед recursion-аар, tabulation энэ шиг дарааллаар боддог.

en.title: Introduction to DP — saving smaller answers
en.summary: Learn states, base cases and transitions one at a time through a stair problem.

blocks.text: You climb a staircase of $n$ steps, moving up by $1$ or $2$ each time. How many sequences reach the top? For $n=4$ they are $1+1+1+1$, $1+1+2$, $1+2+1$, $2+1+1$, and $2+2$. First establish that order matters: $1+2$ and $2+1$ are different sequences.

Generating every sequence recursively is correct. However, the same problem with five steps remaining is solved again whenever a different prefix reaches it. DP is useful because those residual problems repeat, not simply because recursion is present.
Climb $n$ stairs using steps of size one or two. For $n=3$, the routes are $1+1+1$, $1+2$, and $2+1$: three ways. What about larger $n$?

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Define the state in a full sentence: $dp_i$ counts sequences that climb exactly $i$ steps. Future possibilities depend on the remaining distance, not the entire earlier history. That is why different paths reaching the same state can share one computed answer.

Classify sequences by their final move. Those ending in $1$ correspond to a sequence reaching $i-1$ followed by $1$; those ending in $2$ correspond to one reaching $i-2$ followed by $2$. Hence $dp_i=dp_{i-1}+dp_{i-2}$, with the second term included only for $i\ge2$.

Set $dp_0=1$: the empty sequence is one way to climb zero steps. Setting it to zero corrupts every later answer. Processing increasing $i$ ensures all smaller dependencies are ready; that dependency order is the basis of bottom-up DP.
A recursion can split by the final step, but repeatedly recomputes the same smaller answers. Save those answers in an array.
A final step of one comes from $i-1$; a final step of two comes from $i-2$. These groups do not overlap, so add their counts: $\mathrm{dp}[i]=\mathrm{dp}[i-1]+\mathrm{dp}[i-2]$.

Start DP by defining a state rather than memorizing a formula. Here $dp[i]$ counts ordered step sequences reaching exactly stair $i$. Sequences $1,2$ and $2,1$ are different. A state must contain all information needed for future choices.
The last step is $1$ or $2$. The first group extends paths to $i-1$ by $1$; the second extends paths to $i-2$ by $2$. Their last steps differ, so the groups are disjoint: $dp[i]=dp[i-1]+dp[i-2]$.

Base case $dp[0]$=$1$ represents the single empty path. It lets early answers follow the same recurrence. Increasing $i$ ensures dependencies are ready. Memoization computes states on demand through recursion; tabulation fills them in a chosen order.

items: State $\mathrm{dp}[i]$: the number of ways to reach exactly stair $i$.
Base case $\mathrm{dp}[0]=1$: one way to take no steps.
A transition computes a state from smaller states.

At $i=2$, $1+1=2$, representing $(1,1)$ and $(2)$.
At $i=4$, $3+2=5$, grouping new paths by their last step.

Fill states from small to large and return the requested state.

blocks.text: 1. Data: $dp_i$ stores the number of sequences, not the minimum number of moves. Changing that sentence changes the transition.
vector<long long> dp(n + 1, 0);
2. Initialization: counting the empty sequence once provides the base from which all later answers grow.
3. Main loop: increasing $i$ makes the previous two states available. The guard is necessary because $i-2$ is negative when $i=1$.
4. Output: $dp_n$ answers the exact input size. Summing all states would count sequences reaching different heights.
return dp[n];

sections.title: 7. C++17 code and how to read it

blocks.text: The code intentionally keeps the full dp array. Reducing it to two variables is not the initial goal. Counts are stored modulo $10^9+7$, and $n\ge0$ is required.

items: Zero initialization means no paths to a state by default.
The $i\ge2$ guard avoids a negative $dp[i-2]$ index.
MOD keeps large counts within fixed-width storage; the function returns a remainder rather than the exact count.

blocks.text: Section 13 contains a complete runnable program with the same implementation, input format and checked sample output.

The base case at $i=0$ is correct. Assume every smaller state is correct. Every valid sequence ends with either $1$ or $2$, so those two groups cover all possibilities. Different final moves make the groups disjoint.

Removing the final move leaves exactly one sequence in the corresponding smaller state. Conversely, appending that move to any smaller-state sequence creates one valid sequence. This bijection proves the transition counts, and induction establishes $dp_n$.

Modulo does not preserve the exact count, but it preserves the requested residue: $(a+b)\bmod M=((a\bmod M)+(b\bmod M))\bmod M$. Counts grow quickly, so taking the modulus only at the end may be too late to prevent overflow.

items: Define the state before guessing a recurrence.
Setting $\mathrm{dp}[0]=0$ makes every count zero.

blocks.text: Once you can trace the example without looking at the code, write the implementation yourself. Compare it with a simple loop on new inputs. The links offer another explanation; this lesson’s prose, examples and code were written for Erdene Club.

Naive recursion recomputes states and creates exponentially many calls, bounded above by $O(2^n)$. DP has $n+1$ states. It reads one dependency for $i=1$ and only two thereafter, giving $O(n)$ work. The speedup comes from evaluating each state once, not from the label DP.

The program stores $n+1$ long long values, taking $O(n)$ space or roughly $8(n+1)$ bytes. For the final count alone, only the last two states are needed, allowing $O(1)$ extra space. Do not discard the array blindly when reconstruction or multiple-state answers are required.

If $n$ is as large as $10^{18}$, linear time is still too slow. This recurrence admits faster methods such as matrix exponentiation. Always count states, transition cost per state, preprocessing and memory instead of assuming every DP fits every constraint.

sections.title: 13. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Ask which facts about a chosen prefix can affect the future. If the previous chosen colour matters, an index alone is insufficient. Before merging histories into one state, check that they really have the same possible continuations.

Minimization, maximization and counting require different bases and unreachable values. Counting often uses zero where minimization needs $INF$. Writing the state sentence and transition proof before code reveals incorrect initialization and double counting early.

For counting, minimum-cost and maximum-score DP, first define state, transition, base and evaluation order. Minimum DP often needs INF for unreachable states rather than zero. If identical states have different future options, the state definition is incomplete.

Enumerate paths for small n and compare with DP counts.

tutorials.summary: Зөвхөн баруун, доош явдаг grid-д нэг нүдэнд хүрэх замын тоог өмнөх хоёр нүдээр бодъё.

blocks.text: $3\times3$ хоосон grid-ийн зүүн дээд нүднээс баруун доод нүд рүү зөвхөн баруун, доош явна. Нийт $6$ зам. Дунд нүдийг хаавал $2$ зам л үлдэнэ.
Бүх path-ийг recursion-оор үүсгэж болно. Гэхдээ олон path нэг нүдэн дээр ирнэ. Тэр нүдэнд хүрэх аргын тоог нэг удаа хадгалбал цааш хэрэглэхэд хангалттай.
Нүдэнд хамгийн сүүлд дээрээс эсвэл зүүнээс ирнэ. Тиймээс хоёр хөршийн тоог нэмнэ. Grid-ийн эхний нүд нээлттэй бол $1$ замтай; grid-ийн гаднах нүднээс зам ирэхгүй.

Замыг бүхэлд нь хадгалах шаардлагагүй. $dp[r][c]$ гэдэг нь эхлэлээс $(r,c)$ нүдэнд хүрэх замын тоо. Тухайн нүдэнд ирсний дараах сонголтууд нь өмнө нь ямар замаар ирснээс хамаарахгүй тул ижил нүдэнд ирсэн замуудыг нэг state-д нэгтгэж болно.

Сүүлийн алхам нь зөвхөн дээрээс эсвэл зүүнээс ирнэ. Энэ хоёр бүлэг давхцахгүй, бас бусад боломж байхгүй. Тиймээс замын тоонуудыг нэмнэ: $dp[r][c]=dp[r-1][c]+dp[r][c-1]$. Хана байвал $0$; эхлэх нүд нээлттэй бол $1$ — хөдөлгөөн хийгээгүй нэг зам байна.

en.title: Grid DP — counting paths
en.summary: Count paths to a grid cell from its top and left predecessors.

blocks.text: In an open $3\times3$ grid, moving only right or down gives $6$ paths from top-left to bottom-right. Blocking the center leaves $2$.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Enumerating routes repeats work whenever paths reach the same cell. Save the number of ways to reach each cell once.
A path’s final move comes from above or left. Add those counts. An open starting cell has one path; cells outside the grid contribute none.

You do not need to store complete paths. Let $dp[r][c]$ count paths from the start to cell $(r,c)$. Future choices depend on this cell rather than the route taken to it, so all paths arriving here can be merged into one state.

The final move comes from above or from the left. These groups are disjoint and cover every possibility, giving $dp[r][c]=dp[r-1][c]+dp[r][c-1]$. A wall contributes $0$. An open starting cell contributes $1$: the single path with no moves.

When filling rows from left to right, the upper and left states are already available. This order respects dependencies. Counts grow rapidly, so reduce after each addition; modulo changes the stored count, not which paths are allowed.

items: $\mathrm{dp}[r][c]$ counts routes to cell $(r,c)$.
A wall marked # has count $0$.

blocks.text: Follow this detailed trace slowly. At each step, identify which stored value changes and why.

rows: In a $3\times3$ grid with a central wall, begin with $dp[0][0]=1$.
The first row is $[1,1,1]$: each cell can only be reached from the left.
The second row is $[1,0,1]$: the central wall passes no paths.
The third row is $[1,1,2]$: the last cell receives $1$ from above and $1$ from the left.
The answer is $2$: one route follows the top edge, the other the left and bottom edges.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Do not extend every possible path separately. Different paths arriving at one cell have the same future options, so their count can be combined into one DP value.

There are $nm$ states. Each cell checks whether it is blocked and combines at most two completed values, from above and left. Each state is computed once, giving $O(nm)$ time regardless of how many paths exist.
Example: an unobstructed $5\times5$ grid has $\binom84=70$ paths from start to finish. DP computes only $25$ cell values.
This recurrence assumes acyclic movement down or right. It does not directly solve a path-counting problem allowing arbitrary directions.

blocks.text: Use this recurrence when moves are only right and down. Four-direction movement introduces cycles and invalidates this simple order. For minimum cost, take the minimum predecessor cost and add the current cell cost instead of counting paths.

en.title: 0/1 knapsack — take it or leave it
en.summary: Begin with a full 2D table that makes the one-use-per-item rule explicit.

blocks.text: A bag has capacity $W=5$. Items have (weight,value) $(2,3),(3,4),(4,5)$. The first two fit with value $7$, better than the third item’s value $5$.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Every item creates take/skip choices, giving $2^n$ combinations. Repeated questions about the same prefix of items and capacity can be stored in a DP table.
Skipping uses $\mathrm{dp}[i-1][c]$. Taking uses the previous row at reduced capacity plus the item’s value. Reading both choices from the previous row prevents reuse.

This is $0/1$ knapsack: each item is skipped or taken once. Let $dp[i][c]$ be the maximum value from the first $i$ items with total weight at most $c$. Capacity is an upper limit, not a requirement to fill the bag exactly.

Skipping item $i$ gives $dp[i-1][c]$. Taking it reserves weight $w$ and gives $dp[i-1][c-w]+value$. Choose the maximum of these options. Reading both from the previous row enforces the rule that each item is used at most once.

The first row is all zero because choosing nothing is allowed. Learn the state and choices with two dimensions first. When reducing to one row, iterate capacities downward; ascending iteration can reuse the current item and accidentally implement an unbounded variant.

items: $\mathrm{dp}[i][c]$ is the best value using the first $i$ items with capacity $c$.
0/1 means each item can be selected at most once.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Instead of generating all $2^n$ take-or-skip choices, store the best value for each combination of processed-item count $i$ and capacity $w$. The same state has the same future choices, so worse alternatives can be discarded.
The table has $(n+1)(W+1)$ entries. Each entry compares at most two answers from the previous row: skip or take if possible. Constant work per state gives $O(nW)$ time.
Example: $n=20$, $W=100$ gives $21\times101=2121$ table entries instead of enumerating $2^{20}=1048576$ subsets.
$W$ is a numeric value, not its bit length, so this is called pseudo-polynomial time. A capacity of $10^9$ still makes the $O(nW)$ table impractical.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Use it when $nW$ fits the limits. A huge $W$ makes this representation too expensive; a small total value suggests value-based DP, while small $n$ may permit meet-in-the-middle. Exact-weight variants must distinguish unreachable states from value zero.

en.title: LIS — longest increasing subsequence
en.summary: Learn the direct $O(n^2)$ DP first; the binary-search optimization comes later.

blocks.text: Select elements from $a=[3,1,2,5,4]$ without changing their relative order. Both $[1,2,5]$ and $[1,2,4]$ are increasing subsequences of length $3$. They need not be contiguous.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: We could inspect every subset. Instead, save the longest increasing subsequence ending at each index and extend it when a later value is larger.
A single $a[i]$ has length $1$. For each earlier $j$ with $a[j]<a[i]$, append the current value to get length $\mathrm{dp}[j]+1$. Keep the maximum.
A subsequence keeps index order but may skip elements; a subarray is contiguous. This LIS is strictly increasing, so equal values cannot extend it. Confusing either definition changes the problem.

Let $dp[i]$ be the LIS length ending exactly at index $i$. The single value $a[i]$ gives length $1$. For every earlier $j<i$ with $a[j]<a[i]$, append $a[i]$ to a sequence ending at $j$ and keep the maximum.

The optimum need not end at the final input element, so the answer is $\max_i dp[i]$. Understand this $O(n^2)$ DP first. The faster method keeps the smallest possible tail for each length and uses binary search.

items: A subsequence may skip elements; a subarray is contiguous.
$\mathrm{dp}[i]$ is the longest increasing subsequence ending specifically at $a[i]$.

The second $2$ also gives length $2$; equal values do not extend each other.

blocks.text: Rather than enumerating every subsequence, store the length of the longest increasing subsequence ending at each $a[i]$. A shorter answer with the same endpoint is never better for a future extension.

en.title: Monotonic stacks — the next greater value
en.summary: Keep unresolved indices on a stack and find their next greater values in one scan.

blocks.text: In $a=[2,1,4,3]$, find the first larger value to the right of each element. The indices are $[2,2,-1,-1]$.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Scanning right from every index costs $O(n^2)$. A new value can settle several earlier smaller values at once.
While $a[i]$ exceeds the stack top’s value, assign that index’s answer to $i$ and pop it. Then push $i$, whose own answer is still unknown.

We seek the nearest strictly greater element to the right. The stack holds indices still waiting for an answer. Their values are non-increasing from bottom to top, so a new large value can answer several waiting indices.

If $a[i]$ exceeds the top value, index $i$ answers that top. If an earlier greater value had existed, the index would already have been popped, so this answer is the nearest one. Continue checking the next top, then push $i$ as a new waiting index.

One iteration may pop many indices, but each index is pushed once and popped at most once. This accounting is amortized analysis. A nested while loop does not imply $O(n^2)$: total pops across the whole scan are at most $n$.

items: Store indices rather than values on the stack.
Monotonic means the stack’s values stay ordered in one direction.

blocks.text: Follow this detailed trace slowly. At each step, identify which stored value changes and why.

rows: For $a=[5,4,3,2,6]$, push index $0$ for value $5$.
$4,3,2$ do not exceed the top; stack indices become $[0,1,2,3]$.
At $i=4$, value $6$ pops index $3$ and answers it with $4$.
Indices $2,1,0$ are also popped and answered with $4$.
Index $4$ remains unanswered with $-1$. Output: $[4,4,4,4,-1]$.

items: Initialize answers to $-1$.
Pop smaller top values and assign their answers.
Push the current index.

Read $j$ before popping. $ans[j]=i$ stores an index, not the value $a[i]$.
Equal values are not strictly greater, so the strict $<$ test leaves them waiting.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

blocks.text: Unresolved indices have not yet seen a greater value. The value that pops them is therefore their first greater value to the right.
Each index is pushed once and popped at most once: $O(n)$ time and space.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Do not scan rightwards separately for every element. Keep indices still waiting for their next greater value on a stack. A new large value can resolve several waiting indices at once and remove them permanently.
One iteration can make many pops, but each index is pushed once and popped at most once. All pops combined are at most $n$. Adding this to the $n$ outer iterations gives $O(n)$ total time.
Example: in $[5,4,3,2,6]$, the final $6$ pops four indices. Those four pops are not repeated for every earlier iteration: removed indices never return.
Counting work over the whole sequence is amortized analysis. One iteration may cost $O(n)$ even though all $n$ iterations together cost only $O(n)$.

blocks.text: Useful for nearest greater/smaller queries and histograms, but direction, strictness and the invariant depend on the problem. Do not swap next and previous queries mechanically; first identify which indices are waiting for answers.

A decreasing prefix followed by a large value must correctly trigger many pops.

blocks.text: Эхэндээ $0,1,2,3$ тус тусдаа. $0$ ба $1$, дараа $2$ ба $3$-ыг нэгтгэе. Одоо $1$ ба $3$ холбоогүй. $1$ ба $2$-ыг нэгтгэсний дараа бүгд нэг бүлэг.
Холбоос нэмэх бүрд DFS хийвэл нэг мэдээллийг олон удаа бодно. Бүлэг бүрийг нэг төлөөлөгчөөр хадгалаад төлөөлөгчүүдийг холбож болно.
Эхэндээ node бүр өөрийн parent. Find хийхдээ root хүртэл явна; буцахдаа root-ийг шууд parent болгож замыг богиносгоно. Unite дээр жижиг бүлгийг томд холбоно.

DSU нь node-уудыг давхцахгүй бүлгүүдэд хувааж, хоёр бүлгийг нэгтгэдэг. Parent холбоос нь original graph-ийн edge биш, бүлгийн representative рүү очих дотоод tree. Ижил root-той node-ууд нэг бүлэгт байна.

Find нь parent-ээр root хүртэл очно. Path compression буцахдаа замын node бүрийг шууд root-той холбоно; бүлгийн гишүүнчлэл өөрчлөгдөхгүй. Unite эхлээд хоёр root олж, жижиг бүлгийн root-ийг томынх руу холбоно. Root биш node холбоход бүлгийн хэсэг тасрах эрсдэлтэй.

$sz$ зөвхөн root дээр тухайн бүлгийн зөв хэмжээ. Root биш node-ийн хуучин size-г query-д ашиглахгүй. Union by size дангаараа depth-ийг $O(\log n)$ болгоно; path compression-тай нийлээд олон operation-ийн amortized хугацаа $O(\alpha(n))$, бараг тогтмол боловч яг $O(1)$ гэсэн баталгаа биш.

en.title: DSU — merging groups
en.summary: Track connected groups as new connections are added.

blocks.text: Initially $0,1,2,3$ are separate. Merge $0$ with $1$, and $2$ with $3$. Vertices $1$ and $3$ are still separate. Merging $1$ with $2$ joins everyone.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Repeating DFS after every new edge wastes work. Store one representative for each group and connect representatives.
Initially each node is its own parent. Find follows parents to a root and shortens the path on return. Unite attaches the smaller group to the larger one.
DSU partitions vertices into disjoint groups and merges groups. Parent links are internal representation links, not original graph edges. Vertices with the same root belong to the same group.

Find follows parents to a root. Path compression redirects visited vertices straight to that root without changing membership. Unite first finds both roots, then links the smaller group root under the larger one. Linking a non-root directly can detach part of a group.

Only roots store valid group sizes in $sz$. Never query a non-root stale size. Union by size alone gives logarithmic depth; with path compression, amortized operation time is $O(\alpha(n))$, practically tiny but not a strict $O(1)$ guarantee.

items: Find returns a group’s representative root.
Unite merges two groups and returns false if they were already the same.
$\mathrm{sz}$ records a root’s group size.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: A merge does not rewrite every member’s parent: it finds two roots and links one root to the other. With union by size, whenever a vertex’s depth increases, its component size at least doubles.

Sizes grow as $1\to2\to4\to8$, bounding height by $O(\log n)$ even without compression. Path compression then links visited vertices directly to the root, avoiding the same long path in later finds. With both optimizations, initialization plus $q$ operations costs $O(n+q\alpha(n))$.
Example: with $16$ vertices, size can double only as $1\to2\to4\to8\to16$, so union-by-size depth is at most $4$. After a find compresses that path, the vertex is one parent link from the root.

$\alpha(n)$ is the very slowly growing inverse Ackermann function. The doubling argument proves the logarithmic bound; the inverse-Ackermann proof is more involved. This is an amortized bound, not a claim that every find takes one step.

en.title: Kruskal — a minimum spanning tree
en.summary: Connect all vertices at minimum total cost by choosing edges that do not create cycles.

blocks.text: Three cities have edges $(0,1)$ of weight $2$, $(1,2)$ of weight $3$, and $(0,2)$ of weight $10$. The cheapest connecting network uses the first two edges, totaling $5$. This is a network problem, not an all-pairs shortest-path problem.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Sort edges by weight rather than testing every subset. Take a cheap edge if it connects separate components; skip it if it creates a cycle.
DSU tracks components of selected edges. A successful unite adds a useful connection; an unsuccessful one indicates the endpoints are already connected.

A spanning tree is a connected, acyclic undirected subgraph with $n-1$ edges. An MST minimizes total edge weight among spanning trees. This differs from a shortest-path tree, which minimizes distances from one source.

Process edges in increasing weight. Accept an edge joining different components and skip one inside the same component because it creates a cycle. The chosen edges form a forest, whose components are represented by DSU.

The lightest available joining edge is safe. Across the cut separating one of its components, no lighter candidate exists. If an optimum omits it, add it and replace another cut-crossing edge on the resulting cycle without increasing total weight. This exchange justifies the greedy choice.

items: A spanning tree connects all vertices with $n-1$ edges.
An MST is a spanning tree of minimum total weight.

Accept weight $1$: cost $1$, used $1$.
Accept weight $2$: component $\{0,1,2\}$, cost $3$.
Accept weight $3$: all vertices are connected, cost $6$, used $3$.
The remaining edges lie inside one component and are skipped. Since $used=n-1$, an MST exists.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Kruskal does not run a fresh DFS to test for a cycle before accepting every edge. DSU maintains connectivity of accepted edges and checks whether the endpoints already have the same root.

Sorting $m$ edges costs $O(m\log(m+1))$. Each edge then needs root checks and possibly a merge, totalling $O(m\alpha(n))$, plus $O(n)$ DSU initialization. Total time is $O(n+m\log(m+1)+m\alpha(n))$; sorting usually dominates on connected inputs.
Example: $1000$ vertices and $5000$ edges need at most $5000$ DSU edge checks, not a new $1000$-vertex DFS for each edge.
DSU speeds up connectivity checks, but the sorting cost remains. A disconnected graph yields a spanning forest rather than a spanning tree.

en.title: Priority queues — taking the smallest value first
en.summary: Process the smallest or largest value first rather than following insertion order.

blocks.text: Insert $5,2,8$ and remove the minimum $2$. Insert $1$; the next minimum is now $1$. How can we keep doing this as new values arrive?

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Scanning everything for each removal is slow. A priority queue or heap keeps the most important value at top without sorting every other position.
C++ priority_queue defaults to a max-heap. Greater changes it to a min-heap. Treat the declaration as a standard template while first learning the three operations.

A queue removes the earliest arrival; a priority queue removes the highest-priority item. Here smaller values have higher priority, so we use a min-heap. The remaining items need not be fully sorted; only the minimum must be at the top.

The local rule that a parent is no larger than its children guarantees that the root is globally minimal. Insertion moves a new item upward from the bottom. Removal replaces the root with the last item and moves it downward into a valid position.

A complete binary tree has height $O(\log n)$, giving logarithmic push and pop. Top reads the root in $O(1)$. C++ priority_queue is a max-heap by default; the greater comparator creates a min-heap. Pairs are ordered by the first field, then the second on ties.

items: Top exposes the next value; push inserts and pop removes.
A min-heap exposes the smallest value; a max-heap exposes the largest.

blocks.text: Follow this detailed trace slowly. At each step, identify which stored value changes and why.

rows: Push all of $[7,2,7,1,4]$. The top is $1$.
Append the top and pop it; the remaining minimum is $2$.
The next removals are $2$, then $4$.
The two copies of $7$ are separate entries and both are removed.
Output is $[1,2,4,7,7]$. Reading the internal heap array would not necessarily give this sorted order.

items: Choose min-heap or max-heap.

If nonempty, read top before popping.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

blocks.text: A heap restores the top-priority rule after each push and pop; full internal sorting is unnecessary.
Top is $O(1)$, push/pop are $O(\log n)$. The demo takes $O(n\log n)$ time and $O(n)$ space.

items: Do not use the default max-heap when you need a minimum.
Never read top on an empty heap.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: A binary heap avoids scanning all values for the minimum each time. Its parent-not-greater-than-child rule keeps the minimum ready at the root.

Push repairs one ancestor path upwards; pop repairs one child path downwards after replacing the root. A complete binary tree has height $O(\log n)$, so push and pop cost $O(\log n)$, while top reads the root in $O(1)$. The whole heap need not be sorted.
Example: repeatedly scanning for and removing the minimum examines $n+(n-1)+\cdots+1$ values. A heap uses $n$ pushes and $n$ pops, costing $O(n\log n)$ overall.
The demo builds by individual pushes, so construction costs $O(n\log n)$. It does not use the separate $O(n)$ make_heap construction.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Use it when items arrive and you repeatedly need a minimum or maximum: Dijkstra, scheduling and merging. For a single full ordering, sort is simpler. The standard interface does not support arbitrary index lookup or deletion.

items: Duplicates and negative values must be removed in priority order.
Empty input gives no values; a singleton is removed once.

Дараагийн хамгийн бага distance-тэй node-ийг бүх node дундаас scan хийж олохын оронд min-heap ашиглана. Nonnegative жинтэй тул зөв хамгийн бага entry-г авахад тэр node-ийн distance эцэслэгдэж, adjacency list-ийг нь дахин дахин scan хийхгүй.

blocks.text: Edges $0\to1$, $0\to2$, $2\to1$ have weights $7,2,1$. The direct route costs $7$, while the two-edge route costs $3$. Process the smallest current distance rather than the fewest edges.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: BFS ordering follows edge counts. Replace its queue with a min-heap and improve distances whenever a cheaper route is discovered.
Store (distance,vertex) in the heap. An improved distance can leave an older entry behind. Skip a popped entry when its distance differs from the current best.

$dist[v]$ is the best path length discovered so far, initially $0$ at the source and INF elsewhere. It never underestimates the true optimum because each update represents an actual path. Relaxation tries to improve $u$ by extending a path to $v$ with one edge.

The heap extracts the vertex with the smallest current distance. With nonnegative edges, a route through unprocessed vertices cannot improve it: the first unprocessed distance is already no smaller and further weights cannot reduce it. This justifies processing the minimum first.

A vertex may enter the heap with distance $4$ and later with $3$. The old pair remains present. On extraction, $d\ne dist[v]$ identifies an outdated entry and skips it, preventing redundant adjacency scans.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: A min-heap avoids scanning all vertices to select the next smallest tentative distance. With nonnegative weights, a valid minimum entry settles that vertex, so its adjacency list need not be scanned repeatedly.

Each successful relaxation adds one heap entry, and there cannot be more successes than scanned edges. This lazy version also pops outdated entries, but skips their neighbour scans when $d\ne dist[v]$. Total edge scans are $O(m)$; there are $O(m+1)$ heap entries, each costing $O(\log(m+2))$ to push or pop.
Example: if a vertex improves from distance $10$ to $7$, both entries may remain in the heap. The $7$ entry scans its neighbours; the stale $10$ entry does not.
Including initialization gives the safe bound $O(n+(m+1)\log(m+2))$. For simple graphs it is commonly written $O((n+m)\log(n+1))$. Negative edges invalidate the settling argument.

en.summary: Compute every pair’s shortest distance in one table when the graph is small.

blocks.text: Direct distances are $0\to1=5$, $1\to2=2$, and $0\to2=10$. Going through vertex $1$ improves $0\to2$ to $7$.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Running Dijkstra from every source is one option. A small graph allows a simpler three-loop DP that gradually permits more intermediate vertices.
A route using the new intermediate $k$ splits into $i\to k$ and $k\to j$. Keep the minimum of the old distance and their sum. The outermost $k$ loop preserves the DP stage.
We compute shortest paths for every ordered pair. Initialize $dist[i][j]$ to the minimum direct-edge weight, $0$ on the diagonal and INF when no edge exists. Keep the minimum among parallel edges.

The outer-loop vertex $k$ is a newly permitted intermediate. Before it, paths may use only intermediates $0..k-1$. A new optimum either avoids $k$ and keeps the old value, or passes through $k$ and combines $i\to k$ with $k\to j$. Take the minimum.

Keeping $k$ outermost is part of the state definition and proof; arbitrary loop permutations are incorrect. Negative edges are possible, but pairs affected by a negative cycle have no finite minimum. This reference assumes no such cycles and finite additions fitting long long.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Do not enumerate every path. Store the shortest distance for each pair using the currently allowed intermediate vertices. Allowing vertex $k$ compares the previous answer with a path through $k$ built from two stored distances.

There are $n$ choices of $k$, each checking $n^2$ pairs $(i,j)$. A check does constant addition/comparison work, so $n\times n\times n$ gives $O(n^3)$. DP avoids repeated path enumeration, but still checks all pairs in every phase.
Example: $n=100$ gives $10^6$ candidate checks; $n=200$ gives $8\times10^6$. Doubling the input multiplies the work by eight.
The bound stays $O(n^3)$ even for a sparse graph. Adjacency-list shortest-path methods may suit large sparse graphs better.

en.title: Topological sorting — dependency order
en.summary: Order tasks without violating their prerequisite relationships.

blocks.text: Task $2$ requires tasks $0$ and $1$; task $3$ requires task $2$. Both $[0,1,2,3]$ and $[1,0,2,3]$ are valid orders.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Do not enumerate permutations. Repeatedly take tasks with no unfinished prerequisites, then remove their outgoing dependencies.
Enqueue indegree-zero vertices. Removing one decreases its neighbors’ indegrees. A neighbor reaching zero is now ready.
A directed edge $u\to v$ is a dependency requiring $u$ before $v$. A topological order places every edge source before its destination. Sorting vertex IDs does not guarantee this property.

Indegree counts incoming edges in the remaining graph. A zero-indegree vertex has no pending prerequisite and may be placed next. Decreasing indegrees of its outgoing neighbours simulates removing its edges.

If every vertex is emitted, the order is valid. If vertices remain when the queue empties, each has a remaining incoming dependency. Following predecessors in a finite graph must repeat a vertex, revealing a directed cycle. Such a cycle makes the prerequisite order impossible.

items: Indegree counts incoming edges.
A DAG is a directed acyclic graph. Only DAGs have a topological order.

blocks.text: Follow this detailed trace slowly. At each step, identify which stored value changes and why.

rows: For edges $0\to1,0\to2,1\to3,2\to3$, indegrees are $[0,1,1,2]$.
The queue starts as $[0]$. Removing $0$ gives indegree zero to $1,2$.
Remove $1$: indegree of $3$ changes $2\to1$, so it is not ready yet.
Remove $2$: indegree of $3$ changes $1\to0$, making it ready.
Output is $[0,1,2,3]$. The order $[0,2,1,3]$ is also valid; uniqueness is not guaranteed.

items: Count indegrees.
Enqueue zero-indegree vertices.
Remove a vertex and decrease indegrees along its outgoing edges.

sections.title: 6. C++17 code and how to read it

blocks.text: Topological returns a boolean and fills the order vector. On a cycle it returns false and clears order. The graph must be directed.

items: Indegree construction increments once per edge, not once per vertex.
Enqueue a vertex only when its indegree becomes exactly $0$.
On failure, clearing order prevents a partial output from being mistaken for a complete ordering.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

blocks.text: A vertex is output only after all its prerequisites, so the order is valid. A cycle prevents its vertices’ dependencies from all being removed.
$O(n+m)$ time and $O(n)$ extra space.

items: This dependency model does not apply directly to an undirected graph.
If fewer than $n$ vertices are output, do not treat the partial order as valid.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Do not repeatedly inspect every dependency of every vertex to find the next available one. Indegree stores the number of remaining prerequisites, and vertices enter the queue when it becomes zero.

Each vertex enters and leaves the queue once. Processing it decreases the destination indegree once per outgoing edge. Initializing indegrees and processing the queue each cost $O(n+m)$; adding them still gives $O(n+m)$.
Example: $1000$ tasks and $3000$ dependencies need at most $1000$ dequeues and $3000$ indegree decrements in the queue phase.
With a cycle, some vertices never enter the queue. This does not increase the work; the processed count detects the cycle. The analysis assumes adjacency lists.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Use it for DAG dependencies, course ordering and DAG DP. Cyclic directed graphs have no complete topological order. For the lexicographically smallest order, replace the queue with a min-heap of vertex IDs.

items: A self-loop or two-vertex directed cycle must fail.
Every component of a disconnected DAG must be included.

blocks.text: $a=[2,1,3,4]$. Index $2$ дээр $5$ нэмсний дараа $[1,3]$ sum $1+8+4=13$ болно. Update ба sum query хоёулаа олон удаа ирнэ.
Prefix sum query-д хурдан ч update бүр олон prefix-ийг өөрчилнө. Fenwick tree бүх prefix биш, тусгай хэмжээтэй блокуудын sum-ийг хадгалдаг.
Lowbit-ийг эхлээд блокийн урт гэж ойлго. $1,2,3,4$ дээр уртууд $1,2,1,4$. Prefix query блок авсны дараа тэр уртаар ухарна. Add хийхэд тухайн элементийг агуулсан дараагийн том блок руу ахина.

Prefix sum array-д нэг point update олон prefix-ийг өөрчилдөг. Fenwick нэг prefix-ийг binary хэмжээтэй хэдхэн block-оор угсарч, update-д өртөх block-уудыг л өөрчилнө. Гадаад array zero-based, харин дотоод bit one-based гэдгийг тусад нь ойлго.

Дотоод $bit[i]$ нь $[i-lowbit(i)+1,i]$ one-based range-ийн sum. $lowbit(i)=i\mathbin{\&}(-i)$ нь binary бичлэгийн хамгийн баруун $1$ bit-ийн утга. Жишээ нь $6=110_2$-д lowbit $2$, тиймээс $bit[6]$ нь slot $5,6$-г агуулна.

Prefix query $i$ хүртэлх сүүлчийн block-ийг аваад $i-=lowbit(i)$ хийнэ: авсан block-оос өмнөх prefix үлдэнэ. Update дээр $i+=lowbit(i)$ нь тухайн slot-ийг агуулсан дараагийн том block руу очно. Index $0$-оос дотоод update эхлүүлбэл lowbit $0$ тул loop урагшлахгүй.

en.summary: Support point additions and range sums using stored block totals.

blocks.text: Start with $a=[2,1,3,4]$. Add $5$ at index $2$; the sum on $[1,3]$ becomes $1+8+4=13$. Both updates and queries occur many times.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Ordinary prefix sums answer queries quickly but many totals change after an update. Fenwick stores selected block totals rather than every complete prefix.
First understand lowbit as block length: indices $1,2,3,4$ have lengths $1,2,1,4$. A prefix query moves backward by a block length; an update moves to the next containing block.

A point update changes many ordinary prefixes. Fenwick represents a prefix with a few binary-sized blocks and updates only affected blocks. Keep the external zero-based array separate from the internal one-based bit array.
Internally, $bit[i]$ sums the one-based range $[i-lowbit(i)+1,i]$. Here $lowbit(i)=i\mathbin{\&}(-i)$ isolates the lowest set bit. For $6=110_2$, lowbit is $2$, so $bit[6]$ stores slots $5,6$.

A prefix query takes the final block ending at $i$, then subtracts lowbit to leave the preceding prefix. An update adds lowbit to visit the next larger containing block. Never start an internal update at index $0$: its lowbit is zero, so the loop cannot advance.

items: The public array is zero-based; the internal bit array is one-based.
Lowbit, $i\ \&\ (-i)$, is the value of the least significant set bit.
$\mathrm{bit}[i]$ covers internal indices $i-\mathrm{lowbit}(i)+1$ through $i$.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Fenwick prefix queries combine a few stored, nonoverlapping block sums rather than reading every earlier element.

In a prefix loop, $i-=i\mathbin{\&}(-i)$ clears the lowest set bit of $i$. There are only $O(\log n)$ bits to clear. In an update, $i+=i\mathbin{\&}(-i)$ moves to a larger containing block, with the lowbit at least doubling each step. Updates therefore also take $O(\log n)$.
Example: prefix($13$) follows internal indices $13\to12\to8\to0$, reading $3$ stored sums instead of $13$ individual values. For $n=16$, updating internal index $5$ touches $5,6,8,16$.
A range sum uses two prefix queries, so $2O(\log n)=O(\log n)$. Building this reference by adding each initial value costs $O(n\log n)$; it does not use a separate linear build.

en.title: Recursive segment trees — storing split intervals
en.summary: Learn range sums and point updates through a recursive tree. Every node stores the sum of a specific interval.

blocks.text: Let $a=[2,1,3,4]$. The sum on $[1,3]$ is $8$. Assigning $a[2]=8$ changes that answer to $13$. We need to handle many updates and queries.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: An array gives constant-time updates but linear-time queries. Prefix sums give constant-time queries but expensive updates. Store sums of intervals created by repeatedly splitting the array in half.

Build splits at mid, recursively builds both children, then adds their sums. Query returns zero for no overlap, the stored sum for full coverage, and recurses into children for partial overlap. Update follows the child containing the index and recomputes sums on return.

Each node stores the sum of one contiguous interval. The root covers $[0,n-1]$ and a leaf covers one element. An internal node splits its interval and adds its child sums. The tree-node ID $v$ is different from the array boundaries $l,r$; node $3$ need not represent array index $3$.

A query has three relationships with a node interval: disjoint gives $0$, fully covered gives the stored sum, and partial overlap combines the child results. Stopping at fully covered nodes is the main speedup. Zero is the neutral value for sum because adding it changes nothing.

A point update replaces one leaf and recomputes ancestor sums on return. It descends into only one child per level. A query appears to branch, but only the two boundary paths remain partially covered; complete blocks terminate immediately, giving $O(\log n)$ time.

items: Node $v$ represents $a[l..r]$ with both endpoints included.
Root $v=1$ covers the whole array; its children are $2v$ and $2v+1$.
A leaf has $l=r$ and stores one element. $\mathrm{tree}[v]$ is the interval’s sum.
$l,r$ describe a node’s interval; $\mathrm{ql},\mathrm{qr}$ describe the requested interval.

blocks.text: Follow this detailed trace slowly. At each step, identify which stored value changes and why.

rows: For $a=[2,1,3,4]$, root $[0,3]$ sums to $10$; children $[0,1]$ and $[2,3]$ sum to $3$ and $7$.
Query $[1,3]$ partially overlaps the root and its left child.
Leaf $[0,0]$ is disjoint and returns $0$; leaf $[1,1]$ returns $1$; the fully covered right child returns $7$. Answer: $8$.
Set index $2$ to $8$: leaf $[2,2]$ changes, the right sum becomes $12$, and the root becomes $15$.
Query $[1,3]$ again gives $1+12=13$. The left child stored sum needed no update.

items: Build stops at $l=r$; otherwise split into $[l,\mathrm{mid}]$ and $[\mathrm{mid}+1,r]$.
In query, check no overlap first.
Return immediately for full coverage.
For partial overlap, add the two child results.
Update only the child containing the position; restore sums when returning.

blocks.text: Construct SegTree st($a$). St.query($1,3$) gives $8$; after st.update($2,8$), the same query gives $13$. Public wrappers supply root parameters internally.
Read build, update and query separately. First notice that build reads the original array only at leaves. Then follow update’s single path, and finally query’s three cases.

Allocate about $4n$ slots for node indices. These are node positions, not original-array positions. Update a valid position and query $0\le l\le r<n$. An empty query returns zero; totals must fit long long.

items: Build stops at $l=r$, where the interval contains one element.
Child node IDs are $2v,2v+1$; their intervals are $[l,mid]$ and $[mid+1,r]$.
The public wrappers hide node IDs and internal intervals from callers, taking only query boundaries or a point value.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

blocks.text: Leaves start with correct values, and adding correct child sums gives a correct parent sum. Query combines disjoint covered intervals. Recomputing ancestors after an update restores every affected sum.
Build is $O(n)$, updates and queries are $O(\log n)$, and space is $O(n)$. Queries do not visit every leaf: fully covered nodes stop immediately, and only boundary regions keep splitting.

items: The right child begins at $\mathrm{mid}+1$; do not include mid twice.
Recompute parent sums after an update.
Start with point assignment and sum; leave lazy updates and other aggregates for later.

blocks.label: Show answer

blocks.text: Which sums change when index $0$ is assigned $5$?
Check your answer: $[0,0]=5$, $[0,1]=6$, $[0,3]=13$. The right child is unchanged.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Build computes every node once. A full binary tree with $n$ leaves has $n-1$ internal nodes, so $2n-1$ nodes in total: $O(n)$ build time. A point update follows only the changed leaf’s ancestor path, with one node per level: $O(\log n)$.

A range query calls both children, but most branches stop early. Fully covered nodes return their stored sum; disjoint nodes return immediately. At each level, only at most two partially covered nodes can cross the left and right query boundaries. They create a constant number of child calls per level, so the total is $O(\log n)$.

Example: on $8$ elements, query $[1,6]$ takes the stored sums for nodes $[2,3]$ and $[4,5]$ without visiting their children. Only the two boundaries need further descent. Querying the whole $[0,7]$ interval stops at the root.

Logarithmic tree height alone does not prove logarithmic query time. The crucial additional argument is a constant number of visited nodes per level. This assumes stored sums combine in constant time.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Use it for point updates and associative range queries. For minimum, change the merge to min and the disjoint result to INF; keeping zero breaks positive-array queries. Point updates are insufficient for range additions; learn lazy propagation afterward.

items: Test sizes that are not powers of two; recursive splitting still works.
Test singleton and full-range queries and updates at both endpoints.

en.title: Sparse tables — static range minimum
en.summary: Answer static range-minimum queries using two precomputed blocks.

blocks.text: In $a=[5,2,7,1,4]$, the minimum on $[1,4]$ is $1$. There are many queries and no updates.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: A segment tree queries in $O(\log n)$. Without updates, precompute minima of power-of-two intervals for $O(1)$ queries.
Build each block from two half-length blocks. For a query, anchor the largest fitting power-of-two block at each end. Overlap is harmless because repeated values do not change a minimum.

For an unchanged array, precompute minima of power-of-two blocks instead of rescanning query ranges. Let $st[k][i]$ be the minimum of the $2^k$ values starting at $i$. Here $k$ is the size exponent, not an endpoint.

A block of length $2^k$ consists of two adjacent halves of length $2^{k-1}$. Taking the minimum of their minima gives the whole-block minimum. Build only blocks that fit inside the array; these halves do not overlap.

For query length $L$, choose $k=\lfloor\log_2 L\rfloor$. Blocks of length $2^k$ from each endpoint cover the whole range and may overlap. Duplicate values do not change a minimum because $\min(x,x)=x$. This overlapping formula is invalid for sum.

items: $\mathrm{st}[k][i]$ is the minimum of the length-$2^k$ interval starting at $i$.
$\mathrm{lg}[x]$ is the exponent of the largest power of two not exceeding $x$.

Build $O(n\log n)$, query $O(1)$, space $O(n\log n)$.

Static means no updates.

blocks.text: Once you can trace the example without looking at the code, write the implementation yourself. Compare it with a simple loop on new inputs. The links offer another explanation; this lesson’s prose, examples and code were written for Erdene Club.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Precompute minima of blocks of lengths $1,2,4,8,\ldots$ instead of scanning a range for every query. Each new block combines the minima of two half-sized blocks from the previous level.

There are $O(\log n)$ levels, at most $n$ blocks per level and constant work per block: $O(n\log n)$ preparation. A query combines just two power-of-two blocks, taking the level from the precomputed lg table. Hence queries cost $O(1)$.
Example: a length-$6$ query is covered by two length-$4$ blocks from its ends. Their overlap does not change the minimum, so the query reads only two stored minima.
Minimum tolerates duplicate contributions. Summing two overlapping blocks would be wrong, and updates do not automatically maintain this table.

blocks.text: The two-overlapping-block method works for static minimum, maximum and gcd. Build costs $O(n\log n)$ and queries $O(1)$. Updates invalidate many blocks, so choose a segment tree for dynamic queries. Static sums are simpler with prefix sums.

items: Singletons use $k=0$; power-of-two queries may use the same block twice.
Test ranges touching both endpoints and $n=1$.

blocks.text: $72=2^3\cdot3^2$. Энэ задралаар хуваагчийн тоо $(3+1)(2+1)=12$ болно. Эхлээд яаж factors-ийг олохоо суръя.
Бүх тоонд хувааж үзэхэд удаан. Жижиг хуваагч бүрийг давтан салгавал үлдсэн тоо улам багасна. Квадрат язгуураас их хуваагчдыг бүгдийг шалгах хэрэггүй.

en.title: Prime factorization — decomposing an integer
en.summary: Study one concrete number-theory operation: finding prime factors.

blocks.text: $72=2^3\cdot3^2$. This gives $(3+1)(2+1)=12$ divisors. First learn how to find the factors.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Repeatedly remove small divisors so the remaining number shrinks. There is no need to test every divisor up to the original number.
When a divisor $p$ is found, remove it repeatedly. With smaller factors already removed, the next divisor found is prime. A remainder greater than one after the loop is prime itself.

Prime factorization writes $n$ as a product of primes, storing repeated occurrences with exponents: $360=2^3\cdot3^2\cdot5$. Divisors, gcd, lcm and Euler function calculations build on this representation.

For each candidate $p$, divide repeatedly while divisible. At the start of its iteration, all smaller factors have been removed. A composite candidate cannot divide the remainder because its smaller prime factor has already been removed. Thus the output factors are prime even though every candidate is checked.

Once $p^2>n$, any remaining $n>1$ is prime. A composite remainder would have a factor no greater than $\sqrt n$. The test $p\le n/p$ avoids overflowing a multiplication; as $n$ shrinks, the search bound shrinks too.

items: A factor pair $(p,e)$ records prime $p$ occurring $e$ times.

At candidate $4$, the test fails because $4>5/4$, so the loop stops.
The remaining $5>1$ is prime, so append $(5,1)$.
Output is $(2,3),(3,2),(5,1)$. Multiplying gives $8\cdot9\cdot5=360$.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Divisors occur in pairs $p\cdot q=N$. They cannot both exceed $\sqrt N$, so testing the smaller side is enough; there is no need to try every number up to the original value.

The outer loop tests at most $\sqrt N$ candidates for the original input $N$. Removing factors shrinks the remaining value and its stopping bound. Each successful inner division reduces that value by at least a factor of two, so all divisions together cost $O(\log N)$. The worst-case total is $O(\sqrt N)$.
Example: removing three factors of $2$ from $360$ leaves $45$, then removing two factors of $3$ leaves $5$. The final prime factor is taken directly, with no scan up to $360$.
If the original $N$ is prime, it does not shrink, so testing up to $\sqrt N$ is the worst case. This can still be slow for very large $64$-bit values.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Trial division suits one or a few moderately sized numbers. A large $64$-bit prime may require far too many $\sqrt n$ checks; this is not a fast general-purpose $64$-bit factorizer. Many small queries can use a smallest-prime-factor sieve. The contract excludes $n=0$.

en.title: Combinatorics — combinations and Pascal DP
en.summary: Count ways to choose $k$ objects from $n$ with Pascal’s table, before introducing modular inverses.

blocks.text: Choose two of four students $A,B,C,D$. The pairs are $AB,AC,AD,BC,BD,CD$: six choices. Order does not matter, so $AB$ and $BA$ are the same choice.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: We could enumerate subsets. Instead, divide choices according to whether they include the final student.
Excluding the last object gives $C(n-1,k)$ choices. Including it gives $C(n-1,k-1)$. Add them to obtain Pascal’s recurrence.

$\binom nk$ counts selections of $k$ distinct items from $n$ without regard to order. A permutation does count order. The sets $\{A,B\}$ and $\{B,A\}$ represent the same selection and must not be counted twice.

Pick one distinguished item. Selections containing it choose $k-1$ from the remaining $n-1$; selections excluding it choose $k$ from $n-1$. The groups are disjoint and exhaustive, proving Pascal recurrence: $\binom nk=\binom{n-1}{k-1}+\binom{n-1}k$.

$\binom n0=\binom nn=1$: there is one empty selection and one full selection. Outside $0\le k\le n$, the count is $0$. Pascal uses only addition, so modular division is unnecessary. Reducing factorials modulo first and applying ordinary division to $n!/(k!(n-k)!)$ is incorrect.

items: $C(n,k)=\binom nk$ counts choices of $k$ from $n$.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Pascal’s recurrence avoids enumerating subsets or recomputing the same $(n,k)$ through many recursive branches. Store each answer once and combine two smaller neighbouring answers.

There are $O(N^2)$ states over rows $0$ through $N$, each using constant addition/modulo work. The reference also initializes a full square table, which costs $O(N^2)$. Afterwards, a choose query reads one entry in $O(1)$.
Example: for $N=10$, prepare $11\times11=121$ entries and directly read $\binom{10}{5}=252$. The $252$ selections themselves are never listed.
A constant-time query does not make preparation free. The reference stores answers modulo MOD, not arbitrary-length exact integers.

en.title: KMP — finding a pattern in a string
en.summary: Avoid rechecking a matched prefix when searching for a string pattern.

blocks.text: Where does pattern ababa start in text ababababa? At indices $0,2,4$. Matches can overlap. Understand the direct check at every start before moving to KMP.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: The direct method restarts comparisons after a mismatch. If a suffix of the matched portion is also a pattern prefix, that portion can be reused.
For ababa, prefix and suffix aba coincide, so $\pi[4]=3$. Keeping $j=3$ after a full match allows overlaps. On mismatch, $j=\pi[j-1]$ selects the next shorter reusable prefix.

Naive search repeats comparisons after a mismatch. KMP retains information from characters already matched. A border is both a proper prefix and a suffix; proper means shorter than the entire string. Let $\pi[i]$ be the length of the longest border of $p[0..i]$.

During search, $j$ is the length of a pattern prefix matching the processed text suffix. On a mismatch with $p[j]$, the longest remaining candidate is the border of the matched prefix, of length $\pi[j-1]$. If it also fails, follow the next shorter border.

A complete match starts at $i-m+1$. Reset $j$ to $\pi[m-1]$ to preserve possible overlaps. The text index never retreats. Since $j$ increases at most once per character and decreases on each fallback, total fallback work is linear.

items: A prefix starts at the beginning; a suffix ends at the end.
$\pi[i]$ is the length of the longest proper prefix of $p[0..i]$ that is also its suffix.
$j$ counts the currently matched pattern characters.

The next b,a gives $j=2,3$, producing start $2$, then reset to $1$.
The final b,a produces start $4$. Output is $[0,2,4]$; overlapping matches are retained.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

blocks.text: Prefix links reuse a suffix that is already known to match a pattern prefix. No longer possible reusable prefix has been skipped.
Prefix construction is $O(m)$ and matching is $O(n)$: $O(n+m)$ total. Pi uses $O(m)$ space plus output. Total fallback work is linear because $j$ can only decrease as often as it has increased.

items: Do not reset $j$ to zero after a full match if overlaps must be found.
Pi stores a length, not an index.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Naive matching rechecks characters after a mismatch. KMP’s prefix links identify which suffix of the existing match is also a pattern prefix, letting us update $j$ without rechecking those characters. The text index $i$ never moves backwards.

The while loop may run repeatedly, but $j$ increases by at most one per text character: at most $n$ increases. Each while iteration decreases $j$ by at least one. Since $j\ge0$, total decreases cannot exceed total increases. The same argument bounds prefix construction by $O(m)$, giving $O(n+m)$ overall.
Example: with $p=\text{ababac}$, after matching $\text{ababa}$, a next character $b$ changes $j$ from $5$ to $3$, then matches $p[3]=b$. The already-matched $\text{aba}$ is not checked again.
A prefix link can decrease $j$ by several units, which only helps the bound. Resetting after a match is also a decrease. An empty pattern produces $n+1$ positions, requiring $O(n)$ output work.

Хоёр урт $2^{k-1}$ үсрэлтийг залгаж урт $2^k$ болгоно. Depth-ийн ялгааг binary бичлэгээр задлаад гүн node-ийг тэнцүүлнэ. Дараа томоос жижиг үсрэлтийг common ancestor-ийг давалгүй хэрэглэнэ.

Rooted tree-д ancestor нь node-оос parent-ээр дээш очиж хүрэх node; өөрөө ч ancestor гэж үзнэ. LCA нь хоёр node-ийн common ancestor-уудаас хамгийн гүн нь. Tree-д хоёр node-ийн зам энэ node дээр нийлдэг.

Нэг нэгээр parent рүү өгсөх нь өндөртэй тэнцүү зардалтай. $up[k][v]$-г $v$-ийн $2^k$ алхам дээрх ancestor гэж бэлтгэе. $2^k$ jump нь хоёр $2^{k-1}$ jump: $up[k][v]=up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]$. Root-ийн parent-ийг root гэж тогтоож дээд заагийг аюулгүй болгоно.

Эхлээд гүн node-ийг depth difference-ийн binary bit-үүдээр өргөж ижил depth болгоно. Тэнцвэл тэр node LCA. Үгүй бол том jump-ээс жижиг рүү харж, ancestor-ууд нь ялгаатай үед хоёуланг өргөнө. Ижил ancestor руу шууд jump хийвэл LCA-г давж болох тул түүнийг хийхгүй. Эцэст нь тэд LCA-ийн хоёр хүүхдийн доорх хамгийн дээд байрлалд байна, parent нь хариу.

en.title: LCA — lowest common ancestor
en.summary: Understand climbing parents one step at a time, then speed it up with larger jumps.

blocks.text: Root $0$ has children $1,2$; vertex $1$ has children $3,4$. LCA($3,4$) is $1$, and LCA($3,2$) is $0$. A vertex counts as its own ancestor.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: Lift the deeper vertex until depths match, then lift both one parent at a time until they meet. This direct method is slow on a long chain.
Combine two length-$2^{k-1}$ jumps into one length-$2^k$ jump. Decompose the depth difference into binary jumps. Then lift both vertices from large jumps to small ones without moving past their LCA.
In a rooted tree, an ancestor is reached by repeatedly following parents, including the node itself. The LCA is the deepest common ancestor of two vertices. Their unique tree path passes through it.

Climbing one parent at a time costs the tree height. Precompute $up[k][v]$, the ancestor $2^k$ steps above $v$. A $2^k$ jump is two $2^{k-1}$ jumps: $up[k][v]=up[k-1][up[k-1][v]]$. Let the root be its own parent to handle the upper boundary safely.

First lift the deeper vertex using the binary bits of the depth difference. If the vertices become equal, that vertex is the LCA. Otherwise try jumps from large to small, lifting both only when their ancestors differ. Jumping to an equal ancestor could skip over the LCA. At the end, their common parent is the answer.

items: $\mathrm{up}[k][v]$ is the ancestor $2^k$ parent steps above $v$.
Binary lifting precomputes jumps of $1,2,4,8,\ldots$ steps.

sections.title: 7. Why is it correct and how fast is it?

blocks.text: Equal-depth vertices are equally far below their LCA. Jumping while their ancestors differ keeps them below it; after maximal safe jumps, both are its children.
Build uses $O(n\log n)$ time and space; queries take $O(\log n)$. Distance adds the two depths and subtracts the LCA depth twice.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Binary lifting avoids climbing one parent at a time. Precompute ancestors $1,2,4,8,\ldots$ steps away and express large distances as a few binary jumps.

Each vertex stores $O(\log n)$ jumps, each built from two earlier jumps in constant work: $O(n\log n)$ preparation. A query scans the bits of the depth difference, then the jump levels from large to small. Two logarithmic scans still give $O(\log n)$.
Example: a depth difference of $13=8+4+1$ takes jumps of $8,4,1$ instead of $13$ parent steps. The code still spends time scanning the relevant bit positions.
Logarithmic queries depend on the earlier $O(n\log n)$ preparation. The ancestor table does not automatically update when the tree changes.

sections.title: 12. When to use it and how to test it

blocks.text: Use it for many LCA and distance queries on a rooted connected tree. Build is $O(n\log n)$ and queries $O(\log n)$. General graphs lack unique ancestry. In weighted trees, use root distances for path length while keeping the same LCA table.

blocks.text: Хоёр хүн, хоёр ажил. Cost matrix $\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$. Хүн $0$-д ажил $1$, хүн $1$-д ажил $0$ өгвөл $1+2=3$. Нөгөө assignment $3+4=7$.
Бүх job permutation $n!$ болно. Гэхдээ эхний хэдэн хүнд ижил jobs өгсөн олон хувилбараас хамгийн хямдыг л цааш хадгалах хэрэгтэй.
Mask-д $i$ job байгаа бол дараагийн хүн index $i$. Ашиглаагүй job бүрийг түүнд өгч шинэ mask руу шилжинэ. Хэдэн хүн ажил авсныг тусдаа state болгохгүй, mask өөрөө хэлнэ.

Worker-уудыг $0,1,\ldots,n-1$ дарааллаар онооно. Өмнө сонгосон job-уудын set байхад дараагийн worker-ийн боломжууд тодорхой: тэр set-д ороогүй job-ууд. Аль worker өмнө ямар job авсныг бүхэлд нь хадгалахгүй, тухайн set-д хүрэх хамгийн бага cost-ийг л хадгална.

$mask$-ийн $j$-р bit $1$ бол job $j$ ашигласан. $dp[mask]$ нь эхний popcount($mask$) worker-д яг энэ set-ийг оноосон minimum cost. Тиймээс worker index-ийг нэмэлт dimension-д хадгалах шаардлагагүй: used job-ийн тоо үүнийг өгнө.

Ашиглаагүй $j$ бүрт $next=mask\mathbin{|}(1\ll j)$, cost дээр одоогийн worker-ийн $cost[i][j]$ нэмнэ. Set bit нэмэхэд numeric mask өсөх тул өсөх mask loop dependency-г зөв боловсруулна. Нэг set-д хүрэх өөр order-уудыг minimum болгон нэгтгэснээр $n!$ permutation-оос $2^n$ state рүү буурна.

en.title: Bitmask DP — states indexed by subsets
en.summary: Track which jobs are used instead of enumerating every assignment permutation.

blocks.text: Two people and two jobs have costs $\begin{bmatrix}3&1\\2&4\end{bmatrix}$. Assigning job $1$ to person $0$ and job $0$ to person $1$ costs $3$; the other assignment costs $7$.

sections.title: 2. From the simple approach to the new idea

blocks.text: There are $n!$ job permutations. For each set of jobs assigned to the first few people, only its cheapest cost matters for future choices.
If the mask contains $i$ jobs, person $i$ is next. Try every unused job and transition to the mask with that job added. The mask already determines how many people are assigned.

Assign workers in order $0,1,\ldots,n-1$. Once the set of used jobs is known, the next worker may take any unused job. Instead of storing every previous assignment, retain only the minimum cost of reaching that set.

Bit $j$ of $mask$ is set exactly when job $j$ is used. Let $dp[mask]$ be the minimum cost of assigning this set to the first popcount($mask$) workers. The worker index needs no extra dimension because the number of used jobs determines it.

For every unused $j$, set $next=mask\mathbin{|}(1\ll j)$ and add $cost[i][j]$. Adding a previously unset bit increases the numeric mask, so ascending-mask iteration respects dependencies. Merging assignments reaching the same set reduces $n!$ permutations to $2^n$ states.

items: Set bits identify already used jobs.
$\mathrm{dp}[\mathrm{mask}]$ is the minimum cost of assigning exactly those jobs to the first popcount(mask) people.
Popcount counts set bits.

$dp[011]=\min(9+4,2+6)=8$. Keep the cheaper of two assignments reaching the same set.
The other size-$2$ states are $dp[101]=12$ and $dp[110]=5$.

items: Allocate $2^n$ states, setting the empty state to zero and others to INF.
Transition from each mask using every unused job.

blocks.text: Every assignment adds one unused job at each transition. Keeping only the cheapest cost for a mask is sufficient because all future available jobs depend only on that mask.
$O(n2^n)$ time and $O(2^n)$ DP space. Growth is exponential, so this is only for small $n$.

sections.title: 11. Why does it take this amount of time?

blocks.text: Instead of continuing all $n!$ assignment orders separately, merge paths reaching the same used-job mask. The next worker and remaining jobs are identical, so only the cheapest cost for that mask matters.

There are $2^n$ masks. The reference checks $n$ job bits for each mask, giving $O(n2^n)$ time. There are $n2^{n-1}$ actual unused-job transitions because each job is absent from half the masks; including the bit-check loops gives the same bound.
Example: $n=10$ has $10!=3628800$ full assignments. DP uses $1024$ masks, about $10240$ job checks and $5120$ transitions.
This is faster than factorial enumeration but remains exponential. Increasing $n$ by one doubles the number of masks, so it is unsuitable for large $n$.
